# Book III

**All 37 propositions proved in Lean**, every one as Euclid states it, or for [III.12](12.md) as the text states it. 32 proofs follow Euclid's argument, 4 follow it with one or more steps changed ([III.21](21.md), [III.26](26.md), [III.27](27.md), [III.29](29.md)) and [III.12](12.md)'s follows the argument Heath prints; each page says how. In [III.5](05.md) and [III.6](06.md) our tacit rules contain the propositions too, but our proofs never use those rules. In [III.1](01.md) one of our tacit rules supplies a step of a proof of the proposition, and our proof rests on it. [The overlap catalogue](../../docs/reports/overlaps.md) gives each. Our proofs of 17 propositions do not use the parallel postulate: III.1–III.13 and III.16–III.19. The first proof that does is III.14's.

Key to the table: ✅ proved. The Lean statement is *whole*, as Euclid states it; *restricted*, with hypotheses that leave out cases his words admit; or *in part*, leaving a clause to his words. Of III.12, which Heath prints in brackets, the three are said of the text's enunciation, which may not be Euclid's. Each page says how.

**From the centre to the tangent.** Book I drew circles to find points; Book III studies the circle itself: its centre, the straight lines in it, those that touch it, the angles in its segments, the right angle in a semicircle among them (III.31), and the circumferences those angles stand on. A diameter, in Books I and II often a parallelogram's diagonal, is the circle's again (Definition I.17). The pages are laid out as in Book I, whose [introduction](../I/index.md) walks through one, and the decisions behind our statements and words are gathered in [Book III's brief](../../docs/briefs/0004-book-III.md).

**"Let the centre of the circle ABC be taken."** Euclid says it in III.2, where Heath's reference is III.1, and often after. Our foundations give every circle a centre (`exists_centre`). The statements keep named centres where their geometry uses them, and proofs obtain other centres internally. Where no centre is supplied and Heath's reference for the step is III.1, as in III.2, III.4, III.8 and III.17, the Lean finds the centre as Euclid does, by III.1's construction on a straight line drawn through the circle at random (`Prop1.of_circle`, III.1's companion), and keeps the centre alone, which is all Euclid takes from III.1 there. Where Heath gives no reference, as in III.35 to III.37, the Lean takes the centre from `exists_centre`, just as Euclid's words take it, and the argument is his. His reference stays on the page, and each page's certificate sets his references beside the Lean's citations. III.14's statement names its centre E, so its proof takes none. A circle has only one centre, which Book Zero proves (`centre_unique`): the line through supposed distinct centres A and B meets the circle beyond B at P and beyond A at Q; Definition I.15 gives BP < AP = AQ < BQ = BP, a contradiction. III.28 and III.29 take their centres from the given equal circles. Euclid also bisects a straight line, draws one at right angles or copies an angle with no reference from Heath for I.10, I.11, I.12 or I.23; where the Lean takes those steps, it cites those propositions, and the table shows both. System E's Circle 2 and Circle 3 each give III.2 at once; we assume neither, for both are proved after III.2, from it, and no proof here uses either. III.1 puts its middle point D within the circle by Euclid's own argument for III.2 (`Prop1.within`), and the later proofs take that step by III.2, its corollaries or Definition I.15.

**Words, not axioms.** Book III's words are definitions in [`DefinitionsIII.lean`](../../Elements/Foundations/DefinitionsIII.lean), none an axiom. Equal circles (`EqualCircles`) have equal radii, and Heath finds "nothing technically wrong in saying 'By *equal circles* I mean circles with equal radii'" (vol. 2, p. 2). A straight line touches a circle (`Touches`) "which, meeting the circle and being produced, does not cut the circle" (Definition III.2): it meets the circle, but never in two points. We read circles touching one another (`TouchesInternally`, `TouchesExternally`) as Isaac Todhunter does, by Heath's report: they cut nowhere at all. For contact within the inner circle has a point within the outer, and none outside it; for contact without no point is within both. Heath's own reading, that the circles do not cut at the point of contact (vol. 2, p. 3), is defined beside ours (`TouchesInternallyAt`, `TouchesExternallyAt`). After III.13, its three companions prove the two readings the same, for any two circles and any point: one for contact within, one for contact without, and one for touching of either kind (`Prop13.circlesTouch_iff`). So a statement about circles touching may be read either way; our statements keep the whole circles. Circles that cut (`CirclesCut`) meet at two points and each pass within the other. These readings let III.5 and III.6 draw the line through the point within and compare its parts, as Euclid does. III.10 covers circles that merely meet as well, and its last step is still III.5, for two different circles that meet at two points cut one another, as III.7 and III.8 show (`CirclesCut.of_meet`). Definitions III.4 and III.5 measure how far a straight line is from the centre by the perpendicular drawn to it, as far as its foot (`Foot`); for a diameter the foot is the centre itself, and the distance nothing.

**How long is a circumference?** Our foundations have no magnitude for a curve, so we measure a circumference by twice the angle standing on it at the circumference (Definition III.9; `circumference`, `standing`), and that measure is, by III.20's companion `Prop20.circumference`, its angle at the centre (`angleAtCentre`): less than two right angles for a circumference less than a semicircle, two right angles for a semicircle, and more for a greater one. Euclid compares circumferences only in one circle or in equal circles, and there this measure says exactly when two are equal. In unequal circles it would call two circumferences equal whenever their angles are, though one is longer than the other, so every statement keeps his "in equal circles". In III.27 the conclusion would hold without it, since the measure carries no radius, and the proof keeps it on Euclid's route; in III.26 and III.28, which conclude that the circumferences coincide as well, and in III.29, where the measures meet straight lines, it does real work.

**When are two segments equal?** When they coincide, as Euclid's III.24 has them: laid one on the other, end on end and circumference on circumference, with every distance kept (`Arc.Congruent`). A segment is named, as Heath names it, by its circle, the ends of its base and a point on its side (`Arc`). Our foundations move no figure but in I.4 and I.8, so laying one segment on another is proved from them, once, for III.24 (`placement`). III.26 and III.28 then conclude that equal circumferences coincide too, and the theorems after III.29, in [`Arcs.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Arcs.lean), say what equal measures come to.

**"Therefore EF is equal to EG."** III.14 reads it off the equal squares on EF and EG, one of the steps Euclid takes for granted again and again. We prove each once, and the line under each page's table names those its proof calls on. In [`Squares.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Squares.lean), equal squares are on equal straight lines (`BookI.Prop46.sq`), and every straight line has just one foot of the perpendicular from a point, by I.12 and I.17; after III.2, in [`Feet.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Feet.lean), the perpendicular from the centre falls between the ends of a straight line in the circle (`foot_between`). I.47 is said of the squares on straight lines, as in Book II. With the squares of I.46 and I.47, Postulate 5 first comes into Book III, at III.14.

**Two circumferences make a circle.** What Euclid assumes of circumferences from III.24 on is proved once, from III.20 to III.22, in [`Circumferences.lean`](../../Elements/BookIII/Circumferences.lean). A circumference may be measured at any point of the circle on the other side of its straight line, since the angles there are all equal (`Circumference.eq`), or by the angle its ends make at the centre, when the centre lies beyond it (`Circumference.centre`). The two circumferences on one straight line make up the whole circle (`Circumference.whole`). And a circumference is a semicircle, less than one, or greater, as the centre lies on its straight line, beyond it, or on its side. Through I.32, every fact about circumferences rests on Postulate 5.

**"From this it is manifest."** So Euclid opens the porisms to III.1 and III.16, and later proofs cite them: the centre lies on a straight line bisecting a straight line in the circle at right angles (III.9, III.10), and the straight line at right angles to a diameter at its end touches the circle (III.17, III.33 and III.37, and III.34, where Heath gives no reference for drawing EF).

**How our statements are worded.** III.1 constructs the centre of a given circle, with background existence supplied inside its proof. III.9 leaves out "within", which its proof never uses and III.25 cannot grant. III.12, Heron's addition to III.11 in Heath's square brackets, is kept, and stated and proved like the rest. None is restricted. III.7, III.8, III.14, III.15 and III.17 keep Euclid's figure in their main statements, and their companions take every case: III.7 and III.8 compare straight lines on either side of the diameter; III.14 and III.15 measure each straight line to its foot, so that a diameter, at no distance from the centre, is taken too, and III.15 shows the diameter greatest of all, with no more remote straight line beside it; and III.17 starts from any point not within the circle, on the circumference too. III.25 constructs a circle from the base, a point choosing the segment's side, a condition saying which points belong to its circumference and the fact that every ray drawn from within the base towards that side meets the circumference. The construction is given no circle or centre; a companion proves that the circle it draws is the one the segment came from. III.24 lays one segment on the other and proves that they coincide; its companions give equal circles and equal measures. III.16 and III.31 state their last clauses, on angles "contained by a straight line and a circumference" (Definition III.7), in companions beside their main statements, each such angle read as the region it opens near its vertex and compared there with rectilineal angles. III.18 shows that every straight line touching a circle is III.16's, at right angles to the diameter through the point of contact, and its companions carry III.16's comparisons to each: the angle of contact, III.16's remaining angle, is less than every acute rectilineal angle, and the angle of the semicircle greater. Our angle of contact is named by the touching straight line and a straight line from the point of contact into the circle, and near that point it is the same angle whichever straight line into the circle names it (`Prop18.contact_locallyEqual`). III.20 reads Euclid's angle at the centre as the angle standing on the circumference, of any size (`angleAtCentre`), a reading made after Heath's notes (vol. 2, pp. 47–49) and not Euclid's, so that III.20 and III.21 take Euclid's one argument for every case, and III.26 takes it with one step changed: where the angles at the circumference are obtuse, the angles at the centres are greater than two right angles, and I.4 takes the angles that remain of four right angles; its companion `Prop20.special` keeps the statement with the centre on the same side of BC as A, where the angle at the centre is the rectilineal angle BEC, for the propositions that ask for that angle. III.26 and III.28 read equal circumferences as equal in measure and coinciding, which says more than Heath's words. Each of these pages tells why.
